headline: Autumn may be kin to “bright”, “red” and “full up” — though Wiktionary says the exact relationship remains unclear.

sources.quote: ⟨aki1⟩ → */akʲi/ → /aki/
From Old Japanese.

Likely cognate with 明き (aki, “bright”), 赤 (aka, “red”), 飽きる (akiru, “to become full up”, possibly in reference to the harvest), 空く (aku, “to become empty”), 開く (aku, “to open up”). However, the exact relationship of these terms remains unclear.

headline: Fog is a verb turned noun: kiri is the stem of kiru, “to become foggy”.

sources.quote: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 霧(き)る (kiru, “to become foggy”).
First attested in 712 CE in the Kojiki, in the sense "breath expelled from a person".

headline: Dew is tsuyu, and Wiktionary can trace it no further back than Old Japanese.

sources.quote: 露 (tsuyu): a droplet of dew on a leaf.
⟨tuyu⟩ → /t͡suju/
From Old Japanese.

headline: Frost may be the “low” word: shimo is thought to be cognate with, or derived from, 下 (“bottom, lower part”).

sources.quote: ⟨simo₁⟩ → /simo/ → /ɕimo/
From Old Japanese, first attested in the Harima Fudoki of 715 CE, in turn from Proto-Japonic *simo.
Thought to be cognate with or derived from 下(しも) (⟨simo1⟩ → shimo, “bottom, lower part”).

headline: Tree is ki, with a Ryukyuan cousin *ke, and it is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 木 (ki2), from Proto-Japonic *kəi. Cognate with Proto-Ryukyuan *ke. For the vowel alternation, see Wiktionary:About Proto-Japonic § Standalone forms and combining forms.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

headline: Leaf, feather, tooth, blade: Wiktionary lists them as possible kin, then notes that their pitch accents disagree.

sources.quote: 葉 (ha, yō): sunlight through leaves.
/pa/ → /ɸa/ → /ha/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pa.
Probably cognate with Old Japanese verb 生(は)ゆ (hayu, “to sprout, to grow”) → modern 生(は)える (haeru), and with 羽(は) (ha, “feather; wing”).

Suggested in some sources as possibly cognate with 歯(は) (ha, “tooth”), from the way that both sprout and then later fall, and with 刃(は) (ha, “blade”) from similarities in shape (cf. English blade). However, the pitch accent patterns are different; 葉 and 羽 are both unaccented, while 歯 and 刃 are both accented. This may reflect two disparate *pa roots in the ancient language.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE with the phonetic spelling 波.
Cognate with Okinawan 葉 (fā).

headline: A forest as a heap: mori is probably cognate with 盛り (“heap, pile”), from how woods look from a distance.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, first attested in the Man'yōshū (c. 759 CE).

Probably cognate with 盛り (mori, “heap, pile”), the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 盛る (moru, “to heap up, to build up into a significant amount”), from the way a forest can look like a heap or mound from a distance.

headline: A hayashi may have been a deliberately planted grove: the word derives from the transitive verb 生やす (“to grow”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First mentioned in the Man'yōshū, completed in 759 CE.

Derives from the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of verb 生やす (hayasu, “to grow”). The root verb is in the transitive form, suggesting that the original sense of hayashi may have indicated a deliberately planted or managed grove.

headline: Mountain and forest in one: Proto-Japonic *yama meant “mountain; forest”.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 山 (yama). First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Reconstructed as deriving in turn from Proto-Japonic *yama (“mountain; forest”).

headline: Rivers once had a p: Old Japanese kapa is the ancestor of kawa.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 川 (kapa), from Proto-Japonic *kapa.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

headline: A bridge is “the space between”: hashi is cognate with words for stairs, narrow gaps and squeezing.

sources.quote: 橋 on Japanese Wikipedia
/pasi/ → /ɸasi/ → /hasi/
From Old Japanese, originally indicating either the area between two things, or a connection between two things.

Cognate with 階 (hashi, “stairs from a garden up to the house”), both cognate with root hasa indicating the narrow area between two things, as in 狭間 (classical hasama, modern hazama, “narrow gap between two things”) or 挟む (hasamu, “to put between two things that are close together, to squeeze between two things”). Cognate also with root hoso indicating the narrowness of a thing itself, as in 細い (hosoi, “narrow, slender”), 細める (hosomeru, “to narrow something, to make something narrow”).

headline: The road began with a god: mi- (honorific) + chi (“road”), the prefix pointing to the kami of roads.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *miti.
Originally a compound of 御(み) (mi-, honorific prefix) + 路(ち) (chi, “road, street, way”). The prefix mi- was in reference to the 神(かみ) (kami, “god, spirit”) of roads.
Perhaps also cognate with *miti, a potentially road-related element found in Old Korean toponyms.

headline: Machi first meant a “plot of land”, and Vovin argues it was borrowed from a Korean ancestor word for “field”.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, with the original meaning of “plot of land”. Vovin argues it is likely borrowed from an ancestor to Middle Korean 맡 (math, “field”) , but all Japanese etymological theories base the etymology on the meaning of “town; section of a castle town”, typically using 道(ち) (chi), 道(みち) (michi, “road”).

headline: A village is either “a gathering” (from 群れる) or a word from Old Korean — the source does not pick.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *mura.

Either formed from the nominalization of 群れる (mureru, “to gather”), or from Old Korean. In Old Korean toponyms, this appears with the phonetic spelling 牟羅 (*mura). Compare Korean 무리 (muri, “group, crowd”), also possibly cognate with 群れる (mureru, “to gather”).

headline: A station began as a relay post where horses were changed.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 驛 (yek, “relay station (a place for changing horses in pre-modern times)”). First attested in Japanese in 718.

headline: Literally an “electric vehicle”: 電 (den) + 車 (sha).

sources.quote: 電(でん) (den, “electric”) + 車(しゃ) (sha, “vehicle”).

headline: Before it meant “umbrella”, 傘 was a rain hat made of bundled reeds or sedges.

sources.quote: 傘 (kasa): an umbrella.
傘 on Japanese Wikipedia

From Old Japanese. Attested in a gloss of the Nihon Shoki (720) and Man'yōshū (759) in the ideographic spelling 笠. In turn, from reconstructed Proto-Japonic *kasa (“rain hat”). Possibly related to 重なる (kasanaru, “to overlap, to be layered”, intransitive), 重ねる (kasaneru, “to overlap, to layer”, transitive),.

The term originally refers to a bundle of reeds or sedges used as a rain hat. Following the spread of folding umbrellas in the 900s after their introduction from Baekje or China, the sense gradually shifted to also mean "umbrella".

headline: Rain and candy are both ame today, but Wiktionary keeps them as distinct Old Japanese words, ame2 and ame1.

sources.quote: ⟨ame2⟩ → */aməɨ/ → /ame/
From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *amay.
Cognate with 天 (ame, unbound apophonic of ama, “sky”), as in the location of clouds where water precipitates from.
Distinct from 飴 (⟨ame1⟩ → ame, “candy”).

headline: The candy ame is its own word, kept apart from 雨 (“rain”) as ⟨ame1⟩.

sources.quote: ⟨ame1⟩ → */amʲe/ → /ame/
From Old Japanese.
Distinct from 雨 (⟨ame2⟩ → ame, “rain”).

headline: Reconstructed as Proto-Japonic *kansai — with an n that modern kaze no longer has.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kansai.

headline: Cloud is kumo: attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE and reconstructed back to Proto-Japonic *kumo.

sources.quote: 雲 (kumo): an anvil-shaped cumulonimbus cloud
⟨kumo1⟩ → */kumʷo/ → /kumo/
From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kumo.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

headline: Thunder was originally “god” + “cry out”: 神 (kami) + 鳴り (nari).

sources.quote: English Wikipedia has articles on:Thunder and Lightning
Wikipedia Wikipedia
雷 (kaminari, kannari, ikazuchi, narukami, rai): thunder and lightning.
Originally a compound of 神(かみ) (kami, “god, spirit”) + 鳴(な)り (nari, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 鳴(な)る (naru, “to cry out, to call”)).

headline: The rainbow may once have been nuji or noji: the source suggests a shift from those earlier readings.

sources.quote: ⟨nizi⟩ → /niʑi/
From Old Japanese 虹 (nizi), ultimately from Proto-Japonic *nonsi. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Also attested as man’yōgana form 爾自 in the 金光明最勝王経音義 (Konkōmyō Saishōō-kyō Ongi) of 1079. May be a shift from earlier ぬじ (nuji) or のじ (noji) readings.

headline: Many theories for “rice”, from “doing with one's heart” to Austronesian cousins — the last called extremely speculative.

sources.quote: ⟨ko2me2⟩ → */kəməj/ → /kome/
From Old Japanese. First appears in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, with the phonetic man'yōgana spelling 渠(こ)梅(め). In turn, from Proto-Japonic *kəmay.
Many theories exist regarding the ultimate derivation:

Perhaps from 籠(こ)め (kome), the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 籠(こ)める (komeru, “to do with one's heart”)., from the way rice is farmed. The accent of kome in the Heian period is <LL>, while kome- in the Heian period is <L->. (Can this(+) etymology be sourced?)
Possibly cognate with Proto-Vietic *kəːm (“cooked rice”), modern cơm. (Can this(+) etymology be sourced?)

Possibly cognate with Proto-Austronesian *Semay and Old Chinese 糜 (OC *mral). However, this is extremely speculative; none of the known derivations from Proto-Austronesian *Semay develop initial /k/, nor is this shift explainable by any known mechanism within Japonic.

headline: Three theories for sake — “flourish”, “ward off” cold illness, or a corruption of kushi — and none is settled.

sources.quote: ⟨sake2⟩ → /sakəɨ/ → /sake/

From Old Japanese 酒 (sake2), from Proto-Japonic *sakai. Cognate with Proto-Ryukyuan *sake. Attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, with the ideographic spelling 酒. Additionally, appears in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE and the Man'yōshū of c. 759 CE. This is the standalone form of saka- below.
Various theories exist regarding the ultimate derivation:
Might be cognate with 栄(さか)え (sakae), the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 栄(さか)える (sakaeru, “to flourish”).
Might be derived from 避(さ)ける (sakeru, “to ward off, to shun”), from the idea that drinking alcohol would ward off cold diseases.
Might be derived from or a corruption of 酒(くし) (kushi, “rice wine, rice vodka, sake”); however, the phonological shifts required are completely unexplainable.
The final -ke may be an apophonic form of Old Japanese 酒 (ki1).

headline: A pot named for a snack: 鍋 is na (“small snack”) + he (“pot”), with rendaku turning he into be.

sources.quote: ⟨nabe2⟩ → */naⁿbe/ → /nabe/
From Old Japanese, first cited in the Nihon Shoki of 720. In turn, reconstructed as Proto-Japonic *nanpay.

Originally a compound of Old Japanese elements 肴 (na, “small snack, hors d'oeuvre”) + 瓮 (pe, modern he, “a pot or pan for holding food or beverages”). The he changes to be as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Shio is cognate with Ainu sippo, and the Nippo Jisho of 1603 shows it already softened.

sources.quote: 塩 (shio): a close-up picture of salt crystals.
⟨sipo⟩ → /ɕiɸo/ → /ɕiwo/ → /ɕio/
From Old Japanese, cited in the Kojiki of 712 CE. The Old Japanese term is cognate to Ainu シㇷ゚ポ (sippo) and Ainu シㇱポ (sispo).
Cognate with 潮 (shio, “[ocean] tide”).
The medial consonant had already lenited to /w/ by 1603, as recorded in the Nippo Jisho.

headline: Vovin considers miso a borrowing from Koreanic — compare meju — and a 938 source calls it a “Korean sauce”.

sources.quote: ⟨mi1so1⟩ → /miso/
From Old Japanese. First attested in Ritsuryō tax records from 738 CE, with the spelling 未醤.

Possibly also attested with the spelling 末醤 on a mokkan (wooden tally stick) dated to the reign of Emperor Junnin during the years 758–764, although this might be a different word, as 未 and 末 are distinct characters with separate pronunciations and opposite meanings.
Phonetically recorded as 美蘇 in the Wamyō Ruijushō of 938, but the commentary describes this as erroneously written as 未醤.

Vovin considers it to be a borrowing from Koreanic, compare Modern Korean 메주 (meju) "brick of dried fermented soybeans." This is supported by the Ruijushō citing the Youshikangosho saying that it is a "Korean sauce".
Cognate with Proto-Ryukyuan *miso. A Proto-Japonic *misV is sometimes reconstructed as the ancestor for both if Ryukyuan didn't borrow it directly from Japanese.

headline: An egg is a “ball child”: 玉 (tama) + 子 (ko), with ko voiced to go.

sources.quote: 卵 (tamago): a selection of different eggs.
From 玉 (tama, “ball”) + 子 (ko, “child, small thing”). The ko reading for 子 changes to go as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Japanese for “pencil” is a calque of English “lead pencil”, built from a Chinese word.

sources.quote: Calque of English lead pencil, from Middle Chinese 鉛筆 (MC ywen pit)
